summary: JWS normally base64url-encodes the payload before signing it. This standards-track RFC adds an option to sign the payload without that encoding, which can be easier in some uses, especially for large or non-JSON content. It updates RFC 7519.

eli5.summary: Normally a message is scrambled into a special alphabet before it gets signed. This lets you sign the plain message directly when that is simpler.

questions: what is the jws b64 header parameter
how to sign a jws without base64url encoding
can a jwt use unencoded payload
subtitle: A header switch that lets a JWS sign the raw payload instead of its base64url-encoded form.

tldr.problem: JSON Web Signature always base64url-encodes the payload before signing, which costs extra memory and time when the payload is large and is already delivered separately.
tldr.mechanism: A new b64 header parameter, set to false, tells the signer and verifier to put the payload into the signing input as is. The parameter must sit in the protected header and be listed in crit.
tldr.outcome: Large or detached payloads can be signed without copying or re-encoding them, at the price that the application must keep the payload safe for the chosen serialization. JWTs must not use it.

today: RFC 7797 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It updates RFC 7519 by stating that JWTs MUST NOT use the unencoded payload option.

sections.title: Why Skip the Encoding
sections.content:
JSON Web Signature (JWS) defines the JWS Signing Input as the base64url-encoded protected header, a period, and the base64url-encoded payload. That works for any payload, but some use cases found the encoding unnecessary or an obstacle to adoption, particularly when the payload is large or detached.

RFC 7797 adds a header parameter that makes the payload encoding optional. The main use case is a very large payload that the parties already have a way to exchange without modification. Skipping the encoding avoids allocating storage for the encoded copy and avoids the encoding computation, which the RFC says can bring sometimes significant space and time improvements.
sections.eli5: Packing a huge box of toys into a special wrapper before you sign the box takes time and space. If the box already travels safely, you can just sign it as it is.

sections.title: The b64 Header Parameter
sections.content:
The b64 (base64url-encode payload) parameter is a JSON boolean with a default of true. When it is false, the payload appears in the JWS and in the signing input as the raw payload value, with no encoding. Use is optional.

The parameter changes the signing input. With true it is ASCII(BASE64URL(UTF8(JWS Protected Header)) || '.' || BASE64URL(JWS Payload)). With false it is ASCII(BASE64URL(UTF8(JWS Protected Header)) || '.') || JWS Payload.

b64 MUST be integrity protected, so it MUST occur only in the JWS Protected Header. If a JWS has multiple signatures or MACs, the value MUST be the same for all of them.
sections.eli5: A little note on the envelope says whether the message was wrapped first. The note itself is covered by the signature so nobody can change it.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC signs the payload octets [36, 46, 48, 50], which are the ASCII characters $.02. Encoded, that payload is JC4wMg. The control header {"alg":"HS256"} gives the signing input eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.JC4wMg.

With the header {"alg":"HS256","b64":false,"crit":["b64"]} the signing input ends in the raw text $.02 instead. That payload contains a period, so in the Compact Serialization it cannot be carried inline and the RFC shows it detached, with an empty payload section between two dots. In the flattened JSON Serialization the payload member can hold $.02 directly, and a detached version would simply omit it.
sections.eli5: The same short note gets two different signing recipes. One scrambles the note first, the other signs it plain. The plain one cannot be put in a place where a dot means the end of a part, so it is sent separately.

sections.title: Payload Content Restrictions
sections.content:
Base64url encoding kept delimiter characters out of the payload. Without it, the payload must be limited to what the serialization can safely carry.

  • Detached payload: any octet sequence the application can represent. If the application content-encodes it, it MUST say whether the signature covers the encoded or the unencoded content.
  • Compact Serialization, non-detached: a payload containing a period MUST NOT be used. If the JWS must be URL-safe, the payload MUST use only letters a to z and A to Z, digits 0 to 9, dash, underscore and tilde. Otherwise space and printable ASCII other than period MAY be used, if the application can send the JWS unmodified.
  • JSON Serialization, non-detached: the payload must be the UTF-8 octets of Unicode code points representable in a JSON string, after JSON escape processing, so $.02 and \u0024.02 are equivalent. Unassigned code points MUST NOT be used.

Because the allowed characters differ, some JWSs with b64 false cannot be syntactically converted between the two serializations.
sections.eli5: If you skip the wrapper, you must be careful what you write, because some marks, like the dot, mean something special to the envelope.

sections.title: Using crit and Application Guidance
sections.content:
The crit header parameter MUST be included with b64 in its set of values. That makes implementations that do not understand b64 reject the JWS instead of misreading it.

Application profiles should say whether b64 false is used in each context, and apply it consistently. Varying it dynamically between payloads in the same context is NOT RECOMMENDED. Using b64 with true is legal, but omitting it is RECOMMENDED. For interoperability, JSON Web Tokens MUST NOT use b64 with false, which is how this RFC updates RFC 7519.
sections.eli5: A warning label says that readers who do not know the new rule must refuse the message rather than guess. Some kinds of messages, like tokens, are not allowed to use the new rule at all.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Dropping the encoding drops its protection. Base64url kept the period (Compact Serialization delimiter) and double quote (JSON Serialization delimiter) out of the payload. With b64 false, the application is responsible for ensuring the payload will not cause parsing problems, and for ensuring the payload is not modified in transit.

Leaving out crit is dangerous. A receiver that does not support b64 would still verify the signature but would treat the payload as base64url-decoded. The RFC's example is a received payload NDA1, which such an implementation would read as 405. Requiring crit prevents this misinterpretation.
sections.eli5: If a reader does not know the new rule, it could read the message as something else even though the signature looks fine. The warning label stops that.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: RFC 7797 registers b64 in the IANA JSON Web Signature and Encryption Header Parameters registry established by RFC 7515. The description is Base64url-Encode Payload, the usage location is JWS, and the change controller is the IESG.
sections.eli5: The new note name is written in the official list of names so nobody else uses it for something different.
